To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the risk of developing Carpal Tunnel Syndrome is significantly increased for workers with a history of tendonitis and numbness and tingling in their hands, and for workers with high levels of peak force and hand/wrist activity.
the incidence of CTS is higher in industrial and clerical populations, and that a number of factors, including physical and ergonomic risk factors, may play a role in its development.
the incidence of CTS is 2.4 per 100 person years, and the incidence of CTD is 4.7 per 100 person-years.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of risk factors for the development of CTDs in workers and the development of a model to predict the likelihood of the onset of CTDs.
the development of CTDs, particularly CTS, among workers.
the development of an epidemiological model to predict the risk of CTS in the industrial population and to develop an intervention program to prevent the onset of CTS.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the risk of developing CTS increases when the worker has a history of tendonitis and/or a history of numb, tingly, burning, and or pain in the hand and when the worker performs work above the action levels of peak force and hand activities.

the incidence of CTS was significantly associated with a number of risk factors, including physical and ergonomic factors, and that these factors should be considered in the development of preventive strategies for CTS.
CTS is a multifactorial disease with both work related and personal factors playing important roles in its development.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the risk factors for CTR are not only physical but also psychosocial.
there is a strong association between the risk factors and CTS.

the combination of a history of tendonitis, a long median-ulnar peak nerve conduction velocity difference, and a long duration of work above the action limit for peak force and above the threshold limit value of hand activity level is predictive for developing CTS.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CTS is a complex disorder and that the risk factors for CTR are multifactorial.
CTS is a complex disorder that is affected by both physical and work-related factors.

the risk of developing CTS is increased by both physical and psychosocial factors, including a history of wrist tendonitis, a positive history of numbness or pain in the hands, a baseline median-ulnar latency difference, and work above action level of the force and hand activity levels threshold limit values.
